column2: [Bhishma said:] Safety from all beings, help in misfortune, and whatever is wished one should give to the thirsty one who begs.
That is called the best gift, which, once given, the giver thinks well given; the gift that follows the giver, bull of the Bharatas.
Gifts of gold, cows and land are purifiers; they carry across even a sinner.
Give these constantly to the good, tiger among men; gifts free a man from sin, without doubt.
Whatever is most desired in the world and dear in one's house, that should be given to a worthy one by one who wishes it imperishable.
One who gives dear things and does dear things gains dear things in the world, and becomes dear to beings here and hereafter.
One who from pride does not honour as he can a beggar, hopeful and possessionless, is cruel, Yudhishthira.
Invite by every means, Kaunteya, the good who are modest and controlled, wasted by sons and wives, and who do not ask.
Those who make no wish for blessings among gods or mortals, worthy, always set in sattva, living on what comes,
protect yourself from them as from venomous snakes, Bharata; having tested those best of the twice-born by speech,
invite them, Kauravya, with houses always built, with servants and furniture, bringing all desires and comfort.
If they should accept what is purified by faith, Yudhishthira, thinking "It must be done," the righteous doers of merit,
bathed in knowledge, bathed in vows, living in dependence, with hidden study and austerity, brahmanas of sharp vows,
whatever good you do to those pure, self-controlled and devoted to their own wives will establish you in the worlds.
As a well-offered Agnihotra by a twice-born in the evening and morning, so is a gift to the twice-born by a self-purified man.
This is your spread sacrifice, purified by faith, with fee; let it go on, better than all sacrifices, as you give, dear one.
An offering equal to a gift to such men, Yudhishthira: offering and honouring them, one gains freedom from debt.
Those who do not get angry at us and do not covet even a blade of grass are most to be honoured by us, and others who speak kindly.
Those who do not esteem us much and do not engage should be cherished like sons; homage to them, and safety.
Officiants, priests and teachers are gentle upholders of Brahman; splendour joined with kshatriya power is appeased in a twice-born.
I have, I am strong, I am king, Yudhishthira: do not eat brahmanas out of garments and food.
With whatever wealth you have for beauty or strength, sinless one, brahmanas are to be honoured by you as you follow your own dharma.
Salute the brahmanas, behaving as is right; let them play with you as with a son, at ease and as they wish.
Who else than you, best of the Kurus, deserves to cut the livelihood of these very gracious, contented friends?
As the husband's hermitage is eternal dharma for women in the world, he is god and goal and no other, so for us are the twice-born.
If, dear one, unhonoured brahmanas should abandon us, seeing the cruel act constantly in the kshatriya,
then what purpose would life have for us without the Vedas, without fame, without worlds, without sacrifice, for that is dependent on brahmanas.
Here I shall tell you how dharma is eternal: a kshatriya formerly served a brahmana, a vaishya a kshatriya, and a shudra a vaishya, so tradition says.
A shudra should serve a brahmana blazing like fire from a distance, while a vaishya and kshatriya should serve touching.
One should serve those twice-born, gentle in nature, true in conduct and keepers of truth and dharma, who are like angry venomous snakes.
Of the others and others and those beyond, splendours and austerities of the kshatriyas who blaze with splendour and strength are appeased in brahmanas alone.
My father is not dearer to me, nor are you so dear, dear one, nor my father's father, king, nor my self, nor my life.
No one on earth is dearer to me than you, and brahmanas are dearer to me than you, bull of the Bharatas.
I say this truth, Pandava, as it is; by that truth may I go to the worlds where Shantanu is.
May I see the pure worlds of the good honoured by Brahman; to those I must go soon and for long.
Having seen such worlds, best of the Bharatas, I am not tormented, king, for what I did toward brahmanas.
[Bhishma said:] They say that to give to one who does not ask is better, Partha, than to one who begs; the steady one deserves it, not the wretch of unsteady self.
A kshatriya's steadiness is in protecting, a brahmana's steadiness is in not seeking; a steady, learned and contented brahmana pleases the gods.
They say begging is the mark of one without lordship and approaching; begging always troubles beings like a robber.
A beggar dies, and after him dies the one who gives; giving revives him and oneself, Yudhishthira.
Non-cruelty is the highest dharma in what is given to one who begs; invite by every means those who are sinking and do not ask.
If such best of the twice-born live in your kingdom, you should recognise them with effort like fires covered with ash.
Blazing with austerity they could burn even the earth; for they are to be honoured, joined with knowledge, realisation, austerity and yoga.
Offer them worship, scorcher of foes, giving many kinds of gifts and wishes to those who do not ask.
Invite the best of the twice-born, Kaunteya, with built charming houses with servants and furniture, and with other desires.
If they accept what is purified by faith, Yudhishthira, the knowers of dharma, seeing the subtle, thinking "It must be done",
if brahmanas have eaten and gone from houses that raise them up, whose wives wait for them as farmers for rain,
let brahmanas, restrained students, eating the food at the morning pressing, dear one, satisfy your three fires.
Let your midday pressing go on as you give; with cows, gold and garments may Indra be pleased with you.
That is your third pressing, Yudhishthira, the Vaishvadeva, what you give to gods, ancestors and brahmanas.
Non-violence to all beings, sharing in every way, self-control, renunciation, steadiness and truth: let these be your concluding bath.
This is your spread sacrifice, purified by faith, with fee; let it always go on, better than all sacrifices, dear one.
[Yudhishthira said:] I wish to know this truly, Bharata; learned one, tell me, who wish to know, the dharmas of giving.
What is given inside the altar with faith and non-cruelty, what is the highest good in that, dear one? Tell me, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] Terrible action constantly belongs to a kshatriya, dear one; his sacrificial work and giving here are purifying.
The good do not accept from sinful kings; for this reason a king should sacrifice with sacrifices of ample fees.
But if they accept, a king should give day after day, taking supreme faith; this is the best purifier.
He should satisfy brahmanas with goods, then, restrained in vow, in the sacrifice, friendly, good, knowers of the Veda, rich in conduct, character and austerity.
What they do with it will be done by you; make sacrifices sweet with food and fees for the good.
Think of yourself as one who has offered and given by the act of giving; honour sacrificers, and so you will have a share.
Prosperous, give to brahmanas, Yudhishthira, cows, bulls, grain, parasols, garments and sandals.
Ghee for those who sacrifice, and grain-food, Bharata, and vehicles with horses, houses and beds.
These are to be given, Bharata, with effective, light means, knowing brahmanas to be wasted by livelihood and free of reproach.
Provide for them by livelihood, hidden or open; that is better for kshatriyas than the Rajasuya and Ashvamedha.
Thus freed from sins and purified, you will gain heaven, having spent your treasury again, when you rule the kingdom.
Then you will gain Brahman-hood and wealth; guard your own livelihood and that of others, Bharata.
Protect your servants like sons, and your subjects; let your winning and keeping always be in brahmanas, Bharata.
The subjects together would kill a pitiless king who does not protect, who is a taker, a plunderer and a non-giver, as the kali of the kingdom.
A king who says "I shall protect you" and does not protect is to be killed together, like a dog mad and afflicted.
Whatever sin subjects commit unprotected by the king, the king gets a fourth of that sin, Bharata.
Some say all of it, others half, but our view is a fourth, having heard Manu's teaching.
Whatever good subjects do well protected by the king, the king also gets a fourth of that merit, Bharata.
May all subjects live on you while you live, Yudhishthira, as beings on a rain-cloud and birds on a great tree.
As rakshasas on Kubera and immortals on Shatakratu, let kinsmen and friends live on you, scorcher of foes.
[Bhishma said:] Beyond all gifts the gift of land is spoken of; the earth is unmoving and imperishable, a milker of unsurpassed desires.
She milks garments, jewels, animals, rice and barley; the giver of land prospers among all beings for everlasting years.
As long as the earth's life lasts here, so long the giver of land prospers; there is nothing higher than the gift of land, Yudhishthira.
We have heard that earlier kings gave even a little of the earth; all those who enjoy land gave land.
Men live on their own work here and hereafter; the earth, prosperity, the great goddess, makes the giver dear.
A king who would give this imperishable fee, having again attained manhood, would become lord of the earth.
As the gift, so the enjoyment: so it is settled in the laws; one might give up the body in battle or give this earth.
This, they say, is the highest blessing of kshatriyas: we have heard that the earth given purifies the giver.
He who takes the land of a good man does not get land; but giving land to the good, he gets land indeed; and the righteous-souled one gains great fame here and after death.
The enemies of him whose land the brahmins always rule for the good man, king, do not rule the earth.
Whatever sin a man commits, wasted by livelihood, is purified even by a gift of land the size of a cow's hide.
Even for kings of mixed deeds and terrible actions, the gift of land is told as the purifier, unsurpassed.
The ancients thought this a small difference: one who sacrifices with the horse sacrifice, or one who gives land to a good man.
Even having done good, the wise might doubt; this one thing is impossible: the unsurpassed gift of land.
Gold, silver, garments, gems, pearls and wealth: all this, greatly wise one, he gives who gives the earth.
Austerity, sacrifice, learning, conduct, freedom from greed, truthfulness, and honouring teachers and gods do not exceed the giver of land.
Those who died in battle, devoted to their master's good, giving up themselves, the perfected who have gone to Brahma's world, do not surpass the giver of land.
As a mother always nourishes her son with milk, so the earth with all juices favours the giver.
Death's servant the rod, fire's most terrible heat, and the terrible nooses of Varuna do not approach the giver of land.
The peaceful-souled one who gives the earth satisfies the ancestors in the world of the ancestors and the gods in the world of the gods.
Giving land that gives a livelihood to one lean, dying, wasted by livelihood and sinking, a man becomes Shri.
As a cow runs to her calf, releasing milk, so the earth becomes to the giver of land, greatly fortunate one.
Giving land ploughed by the plough, with seed and fruitful, or a refuge, he becomes a granter of wishes.
A man who gives land to a brahmana of conduct, a keeper of the fire, pure in vows, does not go to Yama's house; as the moon's increase arises day by day,
so the gift made of land increases with each crop.
Here are the verses sung by the Earth, recited by the knowers of old, by hearing which Jamadagni's son gave the earth to Kashyapa:

He took me alone; having given me, you will gain me, in this world and the next and then at birth again.
mahabharata:13:61.33	The brahmana who knows this utterance, relying on Brahman, goes to Brahman-hood at an offering at a funeral rite.
mahabharata:13:61.34	It is a great expiation for the cursed and for ill-sacrificed deeds; having done it I purify ten on both sides.
mahabharata:13:61.35	He who knows this purifies, and I know it too; the earth is held to be the eternal nature of all beings.
mahabharata:13:61.36	Having consecrated a king, one should have him hear this tradition; hearing it, he should give the earth and not take it from the good.
This is wholly for brahmanas and also for the king, without doubt; the king skilled in dharma is first the mark of prosperity.
Those whose king is ignorant of dharma and a non-believer do not awake in comfort or sleep in comfort.
Men are always troubled by his misdeeds, and many winning-and-keeping do not enter his kingdom.
But those whose king is wise and righteous awake in comfort and sleep very comfortably.
Subjects, satisfied by that king's good and noble deeds, prosper by their own deeds, with winning and keeping and rain.
He is of good family, he is a man, he is a kinsman, he is a doer of merit, he is a giver and a hero, who gives the earth.
Those who give the prosperous earth to a twice-born learned in the Veda blaze on earth with splendour like the Adityas.
As seeds scattered on the ground grow, so desires earned by the gift of land grow.
Aditya, Varuna, Vishnu, Brahma, Soma, Hutashana and the blessed trident-bearer welcome the giver of land.
Men are born on earth and go to their end on earth; this world is fourfold, being of the earth's quality.
She is mother and father of the world, lord of the earth; nothing is equal to her, lord of men.
On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Brihaspati and Indra, Yudhishthira.
Having sacrificed with a great hundred sacrifices with ample fees, Maghavan asked Brihaspati, best of speakers:
Blessed one, by what gift does one prosper in happiness in heaven, what is imperishable and most precious? Tell me, best of speakers.
Thus addressed by the lord of the gods, Brihaspati, priest of the gods, of great splendour, replied to Shatakratu:

Gifts of gold, cows and land, slayer of Vritra: the greatly wise one who gives these is freed from all sins.
mahabharata:13:61.53	There is nothing higher than the gift of land, lord of the gods; I think it distinguished, as the wise say.
mahabharata:13:61.54	Heroes who were slain in battle, going to heaven, longing to give, do not surpass the giver of land, best of the wise.
mahabharata:13:61.55	Heroes who died in battle devoted to their master's good, giving up themselves, and went to Brahma's world, do not surpass the giver of land.
mahabharata:13:61.56	A man who gives land here protects five ancestors before and six who went to earth, eleven.
mahabharata:13:61.57	He who gives the earth strewn with jewels, Purandara, is freed from all stain and is honoured in the world of heaven.
mahabharata:13:61.58	A king giving the prosperous earth joined with all desires and qualities becomes king of kings; that gift is unsurpassed.
mahabharata:13:61.59	All beings think of him who gives Kashyapi joined with all desires, Vasava, He gives me."
The man who gives a cow that milks all desires and precedes all desires goes to heaven with the gods, thousand-eyed.
Rivers flowing with honey and ghee, bearing milk and curds satisfy here the giver of land, lord of gods.
By the gift of land a king is freed from the sin of kings; no other gift is distinguished by the gift of land.
He who gives the earth to the sea's edge, won by weapons, people speak of here as long as this earth bears the cow.
He who gives the holy, rich-flavoured earth, Purandara, his worlds earned by the quality of a gift of land do not decline.
In every way a king here, constantly wishing prosperity, should duly give land to a worthy one, Shakra, wishing for happiness.
Even having done a sin, a man who has given land to a twice-born casts off that sin as a serpent its old skin.
Oceans, rivers, mountains and forests on every side: all this a man gives, Shakra, who gives the earth.
Tanks, wells, streams and lakes, affections and all juices he gives who gives the earth.
Herbs rich in milk, trees with flowers and fruits, forests, rocks and mountains he gives who gives the earth.
Having sacrificed with the Agnishtoma and others with well-obtained fees, he does not gain that fruit which one gains from a gift of land.
The giver favours ten and the taker kills ten; taking back land given earlier, one goes to hell.
One who does not give after promising, or takes back after giving, is bound with the nooses of Varuna and tormented at Death's command.
Those who support a best of the twice-born who keeps the fire, always sacrifices, has lean servants and is fond of guests do not go near Yama.
A king is a debtor to brahmanas, Purandara; and for the other classes he should carry across the lean and weak.
No one, even a god, should take away land given to a brahmana of lean servants, best of gods.
Then the tears fallen from those wretched and sinking brahmanas, when their field is taken, would destroy a family of three generations.
One who restores a king fallen from his kingdom, thousand-eyed, is honoured in the vault of heaven.
Giving land filled with sugar cane, full of barley and wheat, with cows, horses and vehicles, won by strength of arm,
giving land with treasure in its womb and furnished with all jewels, he gains imperishable worlds, for that is his land-sacrifice.
Shaking off all stain, free of dust and honoured by the good, he who gives the earth is honoured by the good in the world.
As a drop of oil fallen on water spreads, Shakra, so a gift of land spreads with each crop.
Kings who at the head of battle, heroes, ornaments of assemblies, are killed facing the enemy, Shakra, go to Brahma's world.
Women devoted to dance and song, adorned with divine garlands, always attend the giver of land in heaven, lord of gods.
He who duly gives land to a twice-born rejoices happily in heaven, honoured by gods and gandharvas.
A hundred apsarases adorned with divine garlands always attend the man who gives land, lord of gods.
Conch, throne, parasol, fine horses and elephants, flowers and heaps of gold come from the gift of land.
His command is unobstructed and the cry of victory arises; flowers are the gift of land, heaven its fruit, Purandara.
Herbs with golden flowers, kusha grass and golden meadows, a man giving gains the land that bears nectar.
There is no gift equal to land, no teacher equal to a mother, no dharma equal to truth, no treasure equal to giving."
Hearing this from Angiras, Vasava then gave this earth, strewn with wealth and jewels, to Angiras.
He who has this praise of the gift of land recited at a funeral rite will have no share of rakshasas or asuras.
And what is given to the ancestors becomes imperishable, without doubt; therefore at funeral rites one should make eating brahmanas hear this.
Thus the best of all gifts has been told to you, sinless one, by me, tiger of the Bharatas; what more do you wish to hear?
[Yudhishthira said:] By what are they pleased at once, when pleased what do they grant? Tell me, mighty-armed, the great fruit of the meritorious.
What gift is fruitful, king, in this world and the next? I wish to hear it from you; tell me in detail.
[Bhishma said:] Long ago Narada, divine-sighted, was asked this very matter; hear from me, Bharata, what he said.
[Narada said:] Of old the gods with troops of sages praise food alone; for the system of the world and sacrifices, all is established in food.
A gift equal to food has not been and will not be; therefore men especially wish to give food.
Food is the maker of strength in the world, breaths are established in food; by food this whole universe is upheld, lord.
From food are householders and also mendicants in this world; from food life arises, directly, without doubt.
Even troubling his family, one wishing his own prosperity should give food to a great-souled brahmana and a mendicant.
Giving up arisen anger, of good character and free of envy, the giver of food gains, king, what happiness there is in heaven and here.
One should not slight one who has come, nor drive him off in any way; the gift is not lost even to a dog-cooker or a dog.
One who gives untroubled food to a weary traveller never seen before would gain great dharma.
The man who satisfies ancestors, gods, sages, brahmanas and guests with food has great fruit of merit.
Even having done a sinful deed, he who gives food to a seeker, especially a brahmana, is not joined with sin.
A gift of food to brahmanas is imperishable, to a shudra of great fruit; the giving of food is distinguished in a shudra and in a brahmana.
One should not ask a brahmana his gotra, practice, study or country when begged, nor his birth when asked for food.
For the giver of food, food-trees with fruit of all desires come to be here and hereafter, lord of men, without doubt.
The ancestors hope as farmers for good rain: "A son or grandson of ours will give food."
A brahmana is a great being; if he himself begs "Give", whether unwilling or willing, by giving one gains merit.
A brahmana is the guest of all beings, an eater of the first fruits; the house to which brahmanas always go begging,
and return honoured, grows exceedingly; after death one is born in a family of great enjoyment, Bharata.
A man who has given food gains an unsurpassed place in the world; the giver of well-seasoned food lives honoured in heaven.
Food is the breath of men, and all is established in food; the giver of food has cattle, sons, wealth and enjoyments.
He becomes also full of life and handsome, king; the giver of food is called the giver of life and the giver of all in the world.
Having duly given food to a guest, a brahmana, the giver gains happiness and is honoured by the gods.
A brahmana is a great being who walks as a field; the seed sown there is of great fruit of merit.
It brings visible joy to the eater and the giver; all other gifts have unseen fruit.
Know that from food comes procreation, and from food pleasure, Bharata; from food know dharma and wealth, and from food the destruction of disease.
In an earlier age the Prajapati called food nectar; food, earth, heaven and space: all is established in food.
When food is lost, the five elements in the body break up, and even a strong man's strength is lost from lack of food.
Invitations, weddings and sacrifices do not go on without food, best of men, and Brahman here dissolves.
All this, whatever is moving or unmoving, is from food; therefore the wise should give food in the three worlds for dharma.
For the man who gives food, strength, vigour, fame and happiness increase always in the three worlds, king.
The water is placed in the clouds, the auspicious wind is for breaths, and that water in the clouds Shakra rains, Bharata.
The sun takes the earth's essence with his own rays; the wind takes those essences from the sun, and the god Prajapati.
When water falls from the cloud onto the earth, then the earth goddess becomes moist, Bharata.
Then crops grow by which the world lives; from them again arise flesh, fat, bone and semen.
From semen, lord of the earth, living beings arise; Agni and Soma are that semen, and procreation is nourished.
Thus food, the sun, wind and semen are remembered as one heap from which beings were born.
[Marutta said:] "I have been revived by you with these words, Narada; where shall I see Samvarta? Tell me, best of speakers."
Let the king follow the path of the ancient royal sages; for all royal sages the forest is the refuge at the end.
Its masses of jewels like weeds, garlanded with diamond ramparts, with the stream of streets for its current and whirlpools of water, with crossings as still pools.
Some best of men have gained the goal of the Guhyakas, giving up the body, conquering heaven by wisdom, speech and deeds.
